summary: For ages 5–7: Earth has a North Pole (top) and a South Pole (bottom), among the coldest places on the planet, sitting as far as possible from the warm Equator that belts the middle. The core spatial pattern is 'middle = hot, top and bottom = cold' (in general), and the simple cause children should hold is that the Sun's warmth is strongest around the middle and weakest at the top and bottom, where the poles are furthest from the warm middle. Use a turnable globe or ball so top and bottom are physical and spatial, always pairing each pole with the Equator so the hot-middle/cold-ends contrast is built rather than two isolated dots.
misconceptions: The poles are two objects/sticks you could touch — they are just the top and bottom points of the spinning Earth
The North Pole is a country or a piece of land — it sits on a frozen ocean, not solid ground
On a flat map the poles are long strips along the top and bottom — on a globe each pole is a single point
It's cold everywhere far from home — the SPECIFIC reason the poles are coldest is that they are furthest from the warm Equator
North Pole and South Pole are the same place — they are opposite ends of the Earth

activities.title: Find the poles on a turnable globe
steps: Hold and turn a real globe or ball; point to the very top and say 'North Pole', then the very bottom and say 'South Pole'.
Run a finger around the middle band (the Equator) and say 'warm here'.
Say the simple rule out loud: 'middle is hot, top and bottom are cold.'
activities.insight: The poles are the top and bottom points of the Earth, and the Equator is the warm belt around the middle — a single spatial frame, not three unrelated facts.

activities.title: Why are the poles so cold?
steps: With a finger on the warm Equator, trace an arrow outward to a pole and say the pole is the furthest place from the warm middle.
Answer: 'Are the poles the hottest or the coldest places on Earth?' and explain why in your own words.
Move a finger from the North Pole down towards the Equator and say whether it gets warmer or colder along the way.
activities.insight: The poles are so cold because the Sun's warmth is weakest at the top and bottom of the Earth, as far as possible from the Equator, where it is strongest. They are not random cold spots, and they are not cold because of being nearer to or further from the Sun.

activities.title: Drag-to-spin exploration (optional interactive scaffold)
steps: Drag to spin a globe, stopping to tap the top, the bottom, and the middle band.
Watch a hot-to-cold colour band shift from red at the Equator to blue at the caps as you look from middle to ends.
Lift a flap or reveal panel asking 'Why are the poles so cold?' and read the arrow tracing from warm middle out to a pole.
activities.insight: Actively rotating to find and tap each pole, with live colour feedback from hot middle to cold ends, reinforces where the poles are and why they are cold.

checkQuestion: Point to the North Pole and the South Pole on this globe. Now tell me: is it hotter or colder at the poles than where the Equator is drawn round the middle — and WHY do you think the poles are the way they are?
checkAnswer: The child points to the top (North Pole) and bottom (South Pole) of the globe and says the poles are much COLDER than the Equator. The reason a young child should give: the poles are as far as you can get from the Equator (the warm middle of the Earth), so they get the least warmth from the Sun and are the coldest places on the planet. (The deeper reason — sunlight hitting at a low, slanting angle — comes later; here, 'farthest from the warm middle' is the target.)
